guide.title: The production design separates finding a logo from deciding which brand it represents.
guide.problem: Marketplace scale makes manual image verification expensive, while product appearance alone often cannot distinguish brands. The system must also handle an open world where most images do not belong to any of the seven initially supported brands.
guide.core_idea: Use YOLO v3 through Darknet to localize candidate logo regions, then pass those crops to a ResNet classifier for more accurate brand prediction. The model acts as an early signal for content QC rather than an unquestioned replacement for human decisions.
guide.outcome: Darknet reaches 91.73% mAP at IoU 0.5 in the reported validation. On 10,000 unknown production images, adding ResNet reduces mistaken assignment to the seven known brands from 2.18% to 0.26%; the combined system reports a 94.01% average F1 score on the mixed evaluation set.
takeaways: Decomposing localization and classification lets each model solve the task it handles best and exposes separate failure modes.
Closed-set accuracy is not enough for marketplace moderation. Unknown brands and images without logos dominate the production distribution.
A human-in-the-loop recommender can create value before recall is high enough for fully automated rejection.
Request-level agreement with QC decisions is a more operational metric than image-level accuracy alone.
False negatives remain difficult when logos are modified, obscured or removed; the product workflow must make that limitation explicit.
review_lenses: Threshold policy: use different confidence thresholds for suggestion, manual review and automatic action.
Open-set monitoring: track unknown-brand false positives separately from confusion among supported brands.
Dataset health: review seller, category and image-style bias as the marketplace and manipulation tactics change.
Feedback loop: distinguish verified QC labels from noisy historical decisions before retraining.
